summary: Hong Kong police said a suspected fraud syndicate used at least 21 identity cards reported lost to apply online for bank accounts at several banks between March 2024 and February 2025. Its members allegedly altered the card portraits, in some applications blending their own facial features into the cardholder’s image with AI, and submitted selfies to pass remote identity checks. Of 44 account applications, 30 passed verification and opened accounts; police attributed 15 of those successful openings to AI face swapping. The accounts were then used for loans and credit-card spending involving about HK$860,000 and for handling more than HK$1.2 million in suspected criminal proceeds. Police arrested six men and two women in April 2025 and seized electronic devices. The reported amounts describe credit activity and suspected proceeds, not a proven loss to every cardholder or bank.

taxonomy_classification.classification_basis: The reported 15 AI face-swap account openings retain Inferential Evidence–Authority Separation: facial verification was promoted to account-opening authority without cardholder entitlement. Identity-Representation Authority Separation also applies because the suspects used real lost-cardholder portraits as the source for unauthorised AI identity composites. The class expressly covers a requester possessing and transforming an identifiable person’s representation, and does not require identifying the generation service. Economic Solicitation Authenticity remains unestablished for the AI subset: the accounts were later used for loans and card spending at syndicate level, but the report does not show that an AI-assisted account was used in a specific loan/payment solicitation or that the composite materially supplied its economic premise. Account opening alone is an access/identity decision; do not equate it automatically with an economic transfer.

primary_classification.classification_basis: Police-sourced reporting attributes 15 successful remote account openings to AI face swaps made from lost identity cards. The facial verification state was accepted as sufficient for account access in the names of people who had not authorised those applicants; independent identity entitlement was absent. This conclusion concerns the reported governance boundary, not an inferred internal classifier defect.

secondary_classifications.classification_basis: Police-sourced reporting describes suspects taking lost, identifiable cardholders’ ID portraits, blending their own facial features into those portraits with AI, and submitting the resulting identity-bound composites without the holders’ authority. The requester possessed and used the likeness as sufficient basis for an unauthorised transformation. The class recognises requester-side as well as system-side authority conflation; a private generator trace is not required.

assessment_boundaries: The April 2025 police briefing is available through contemporaneous reporting; the underlying identity cards, application files, bank decisions and police case file were not reviewed.
The 30 successful account applications include 15 reported AI face-swap successes; the other successful applications cannot be attributed to AI from this evidence.

HK$860,000 describes reported loans and card spending, and more than HK$1.2 million describes suspected proceeds handled through the accounts. Neither is a verified net loss or amount recoverable from the AI-assisted subset.
The June 2026 Legislative Council reply about a 19-account October 2025 operation concerns a distinct syndicate and is excluded from this Case File.
vigil_assessment.factual_basis: The AI Incident Database indexes the case but relies on reporting rather than providing the application files or bank verification logs. HK01’s account of the 19 April 2025 police briefing supplies the application period (March 2024–February 2025), at least 21 lost cards, 44 applications and 30 opened accounts. It distinguishes 15 successful openings involving AI face swapping from other altered-photo methods; all 30 should not be described as AI successes. HK01 reports that investigators received intelligence in February 2025, arrested eight suspected members in April, and described loans and card spending involving approximately HK$860,000 and laundering of more than HK$1.2 million in suspected proceeds. The South China Morning Post independently reports the police briefing and arrests. The exact bank controls, the identity of affected cardholders, final charges or convictions, recoveries, and ultimate allocation of economic loss remain unestablished. A June 2026 Hong Kong Government reply describes a different October 2025 operation with 19 accounts and must not be merged into this occurrence.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: Police-sourced reporting establishes that AI face-swapped card portraits passed online checks in 15 account openings, converting a facial-verification result into consequential account-opening authority for someone other than the cardholder. The same reports establish a separate identity-representation failure: the suspects possessed lost cards bearing identifiable portraits and used those portraits as input for unauthorised AI composites. This class covers requester-side misuse; the generator’s private consent controls need not be identified. The financial activity is reported at syndicate level, so no particular loan or card transaction is assigned to the 15 AI-assisted accounts.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: The suspects used lost cardholders’ portraits as material for new false identity documents and used some resulting AI face composites to pass remote bank onboarding. Those are distinct authority boundaries: permission to transform a person’s likeness and entitlement to open an account in that person’s name. The evidence identifies 15 AI-assisted account openings without isolating later loan amounts to those accounts.
